handbook.title: The Constitution
handbook.intro: A handbook to every number in the game. Values shown are for your current difficulty ({{difficulty}}).
handbook.noMatch: Nothing in the handbook matches that search.

winning.title: Winning: re-election
winning.body: A term lasts {{termYears}} years. On 1 January after the fifth year the voters decide: your approval, moved up to {{swing}} points either way by the campaign, must reach {{reelection}}%. Voter fatigue makes it harder each year: it costs {{fatigue}} points of approval for every year in office after the first, up to {{fatigueMax}}. Win and you may stay on in endless mode, with no further elections.

losing.title: Losing the presidency
losing.body: Parliament impeaches you after {{impeachmentMonths}} months below {{impeachment}}% approval. Generals may stage a coup when coup risk passes {{coup}}. An assassination can succeed if presidential safety is low. Debt above {{bankruptcy}}% of GDP for {{bankruptcyMonths}} months is bankruptcy. A lost war or a nuclear exchange also ends the game, and so does losing the election.

time.title: Time
time.body: One tick is one day. At 1× a day passes every second; 2× and 4× go faster. The clock pauses by itself when a decision or a critical report arrives. Months close on the 1st (the economy and approval settle then) and years on 1 January.

difficulty.title: Difficulty
difficulty.body: Easy, Normal and Hard change the opening treasury and approval, how often crises strike and how hard they land, how warlike the neighbours are, how fast voter fatigue builds and the impeachment threshold. On {{difficulty}}: voter fatigue −{{fatigue}} a year and impeachment below {{impeachment}}%.

options.title: Game options
options.body: Chosen on the New Game screen. No wars: no country can attack India and India cannot declare war. No riots: unrest is held at {{riotCap}}, below every riot. Guided tutorial: a tour of the first month with a practice decision.

approval.title: Approval
approval.body: How the public rates the President, 0–100%. Each month it moves 15% of the way toward a target: the weighted voter satisfaction plus modifiers (ideology, events, scandals, wars, voter fatigue). The “Why?” tooltip on the Dashboard lists every part.

satisfaction.title: Voter satisfaction
satisfaction.body: Voters score eight things from 0 to 100: jobs, prices, growth, corruption, living standards, taxes, public services and safety. Jobs and prices weigh most. The Dashboard's top issues are the three they like least.

treasury.title: Treasury
treasury.body: Cash in ₹ crore. Each month revenue comes in and spending goes out. Deficits are borrowed and add to the debt; surplus cash above a reserve repays it.

budget.title: Budget
budget.body: Department allocations are a share of GDP. Underfunded departments are less efficient, which weakens everything they do, and months of underfunding cost them service stars. A new budget can be enacted at most once every 30 days; announcing large tax rises costs approval at once.

taxes.title: Taxes
taxes.body: Income tax, corporate tax, GST and customs. Higher rates raise revenue but slow growth and annoy voters. Each budget can move a rate by at most 5 points. Trade contracts add to customs revenue.

gdp.title: GDP and growth
gdp.body: The economy is the sum of five sectors: agriculture, industry, services, energy and technology. Real growth comes from investment, department efficiency, stability, corruption drag, the tax burden, your strategy and events. The Economy screen's “Why?” shows each driver.

inflation.title: Inflation
inflation.body: How fast prices rise. Deficit spending, fast growth and shocks push it up. Voters hate rising prices more than almost anything else.

unemployment.title: Unemployment
unemployment.body: The share of people without work. Growth brings it down, recessions push it up. It is the heaviest factor in approval and a cause of unrest.

debt.title: Debt
debt.body: Public debt as a share of GDP. Interest rises as debt grows. Above {{bankruptcy}}% for {{bankruptcyMonths}} months, the country defaults and the presidency ends.

corruption.title: Corruption
corruption.body: A national index from 0 (clean) to 100. It leaks budget money, drags on growth and angers voters. Weak anti-corruption services let petty corruption spread; better ones and audits bring it down.

hdi.title: Human Development Index
hdi.body: Living standards from 0 to 1, built from health, education and income. Health and education spending raise it slowly; voters notice.

sectors.title: Sectors
sectors.body: Each sector grows at its own rate. Your development strategy favours some sectors, and trade contracts boost the sector they cover for their term.

ministries.title: Departments
ministries.body: Eleven departments do the work: Finance, Home Affairs, Defence, External Affairs, Health, Education, Agriculture, Industry, Disaster Management, Intelligence and Anti-Corruption. Each one's efficiency is its funding × the quality of its services × national corruption.

services.title: Services and stars
services.body: Each department runs three or four services, each rated from one to five stars. Upgrading a service costs money once and takes about a month; two stars is where every service starts. Stars last only while the department is funded: after months of heavy underfunding its best service loses one. A few services matter beyond their department: army command keeps the forces loyal, presidential protection keeps you safe, and the intelligence services run operations abroad.

ideology.title: Ideology
ideology.body: Your government's outlook gives lasting modifiers to the economy, approval and diplomacy, and colours how other countries see India. Changing it costs approval and is possible once a year.

strategy.title: Development strategy
strategy.body: Agrarian, industrial, services and technology, defence-first or balanced. It shifts growth between sectors. Changing it costs a little approval and is possible once a year.

events.title: Events and decisions
events.body: Disasters, scandals, protests, threats and diplomatic moments arrive at random. Decisions wait in the inbox with a deadline; each choice lists its exact effects. Letting a crisis lapse applies the default choice and costs approval. A random event happens at most {{repeats}} times in five years.

unrest.title: Unrest
unrest.body: Each of six regions has unrest from 0 to 100, driven by jobs, prices, corruption, approval and policing. From {{tense}} a region is tense; from {{riot}} it riots, which costs growth and approval. Unrest is about regions and causes, never communities.

terror.title: Terror threat
terror.body: A national threat from 0 to 100. Intelligence funding keeps it down. Plots that slip through are announced as warnings and strike unless you act.

operations.title: Counter-terror operations
operations.body: Raids hit cells at once but can go wrong. Surveillance works slowly and quietly. Sealing the border cuts the threat sharply but hurts trade. Each costs money and needs a pause before it can be repeated.

investigations.title: Audits
investigations.body: The Anti-Corruption bureau can audit a department. If it finds misuse, the officials responsible are suspended, corruption falls and the department stays cleaner for a year.

borderTension.title: Border tension
borderTension.body: How tense India's borders are, set by the most hostile neighbour. Good relations and strong deterrence keep it low; war drives it to the top.

coup.title: Army loyalty and coup risk
coup.body: The armed forces' loyalty follows their funding, the army command's confidence and your approval. Low loyalty raises coup risk; above {{coup}}, a coup can happen in any month.

safety.title: Presidential safety
safety.body: How well you are protected, from Home Affairs and Intelligence funding and the presidential protection service. A high terror threat brings attempts; low safety lets them succeed.

forces.title: Armed forces
forces.body: Twelve unit types across land, air and sea, each with a price, monthly upkeep and combat power. The Armoury buys them with treasury money and delivers within weeks; the Defence budget pays the forces' upkeep, and research and drills are paid from the treasury too. Decommissioning units saves their upkeep.

readiness.title: Readiness and morale
readiness.body: Readiness is how quickly the forces could fight today; morale is their will to fight. Both multiply military strength. Drills raise them; underfunding and spy probes lower them.

deterrence.title: Deterrence
deterrence.body: How strongly neighbours are put off attacking. Strength, readiness, drills and nuclear weapons build it. Rival nations weigh it before they threaten or invade.

research.title: Research
research.body: Each domain (land, air, sea, strategic) has three technology tiers. Higher tiers make units stronger but costlier to buy and keep.

drills.title: Drills
drills.body: Land, air, naval and joint exercises cost money and time, and raise readiness, morale and deterrence. Accidents can happen.

intelligence.title: Intelligence and fog of war
intelligence.body: You never see a rival's true strength. Recon gives a snapshot that ages; sabotage weakens a rival but angers it if exposed; counter-intelligence protects India from their spies.

war.title: War
war.body: Wars are fought on fronts named for their terrain, a little every day. Victory can bring annexation or reparations; a stalemate can end in a ceasefire. Wars cost lives, money and approval as weariness grows. India can fight at most two wars at once.

nuclear.title: Nuclear programme
nuclear.body: Research, then enrichment, then warheads. Warheads add a great deal of deterrence. Using one is a catastrophe: the world turns on India, and on Hard it ends the presidency.

relations.title: Relations
relations.body: Every country's attitude to India, from −100 to +100. Each month it drifts toward a target built from its starting attitude, ideology match, treaties, your reputation, recent incidents and world tension. The Country panel's “Why?” shows each part.

reputation.title: Reputation
reputation.body: India's standing in the world, 0–100. Breaking a pact or contract costs it dearly; honoured treaties, embassies and aid rebuild it slowly. It shifts every relation and the odds of every deal.

tension.title: World tension
tension.body: How tense the world is, 0–100. Crises between other countries and global shocks raise it; it cools over time. High tension sours every relation.

trade.title: Trade contracts
trade.body: A contract boosts one sector of India's economy and customs revenue for one, three or five years. Acceptance is a roll with odds shown in advance. You can hold up to {{maxTrade}} contracts at once.

pacts.title: Non-aggression pacts
pacts.body: A pact lasts {{pactYears}} years. While it holds, that country cannot declare war on India. Breaking it costs heavy reputation.

measures.title: Embassies, aid and sanctions
measures.body: Embassies cost ₹400 crore and ₹15 crore a month, and improve relations and deal odds. Aid trades money for goodwill and reputation. Sanctions end trade with a country and hurt both sides.

aiNations.title: Other nations
aiNations.body: Twenty major nations decide each month whether to offer a deal, seek a pact, threaten, sanction or (for rivals) go to war, weighing their relation, relative power, ideology and your deterrence. Offers wait {{offerDays}} days for your answer.

why.title: “Why?” tooltips
why.body: Every key number has a “Why?” that lists exactly what moves it. They use the same formulas as the simulation, so they never disagree with the game.

inbox.title: Inbox
inbox.body: Reports, crises and decisions arrive in the inbox, filtered by category. Unread items are marked; decisions show how many days are left.

saves.title: Saving
saves.body: Five save slots plus an autosave at the end of every month. On the desktop, saves are written safely to your user folder and the last three autosaves are kept.
